Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can be improved at inference time without modifying weights, but existing approaches either apply correction unconditionally or invest in multi-sample selection without learned correction.
We propose ACR-VLA, a lightweight adaptive correction pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. At each control step, the pipeline draws $K{=}2$ action samples in a single batched forward pass and uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance ($\rho{=}0.9979$ vs.\ $K{=}10$ sample variance) as a per-step uncertainty gate. Low-uncertainty steps output the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; high-uncertainty steps apply bounded residual correction via a Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters). Batched $K{=}2$ matches single-sample latency (${\sim}$170\,ms), making the uncertainty signal computationally free.
On SmolVLA (0.4B) across four LIBERO suites, unconditional CRM correction is unstable ($+$1.1\,pp Spatial but $-$1.3\,pp Object, $-$1.5\,pp Long). ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers correction only on high-uncertainty steps (4--20\%), improving performance where the VLA is uncertain ($+$2.1\,pp Spatial, $+$1.3\,pp Goal, 3 seeds; $+$1.0\,pp Long, 1 seed) while remaining neutral on Object ($\Delta{=}0.0$, gating correctly abstains). ACR-VLA uses $5{\times}$ fewer VLA forward passes than $K{=}10$ methods. The key finding is that \emph{gating}---knowing when to correct---is the mechanism: selective correction outperforms both unconditional correction and selection-only approaches. A boundary analysis on a deterministic VLA (OpenVLA-OFT 7B) confirms that stochastic action diversity is a prerequisite.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\looseness=-1 Deploying a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model on a new task usually requires fine-tuning on task demonstrations, yet collecting that data is expensive and the resulting checkpoint may not transfer further. A more attractive route keeps the VLA frozen and improves action quality at inference time. Flow-matching VLAs~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} are well suited to this setting because each forward pass produces a stochastic action sample, enabling multi-sample selection and correction without retraining~\cite{snell2024scaling}. The naive approach draws $K{=}10$ samples and applies unconditional correction at every step, but most control steps are easy---and we show that correcting them adds noise without benefit.

\looseness=-1 Recent work touches parts of this question without answering it. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns a correction head on action chunks but applies it unconditionally and addresses temporal staleness rather than initial action quality. ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} quantifies uncertainty over frozen VLAs but does not learn a corrective residual. SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} uses reinforcement learning and therefore does not stay weight-frozen. VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} performs evolutionary search at $2.41$\,s per control step, ruling out closed-loop deployment. None address the core question: can a frozen VLA decide \emph{per step} whether it needs correction at all?

\looseness=-1 We propose \textbf{ACR-VLA}, an adaptive inference-time pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. ACR-VLA draws only $K{=}2$ samples in a single batched forward pass and uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance as a per-step uncertainty probe. This probe is well-calibrated: Spearman $\rho{=}0.9979$ against $K{=}10$ sample variance, whereas three alternatives all yield $\rho \leq 0.15$. When the probe falls below a threshold $\tau$, the pipeline outputs the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; when it exceeds $\tau$, a lightweight Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters, $<\!1\%$ of the backbone) applies a bounded residual.

\looseness=-1 On SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} (0.4B) across four LIBERO suites~\cite{liu2023libero}, unconditional CRM correction ($\varepsilon{=}0.05$) is unstable: $+$1.1\,pp on Spatial but $-$1.3\,pp on Object and $-$1.5\,pp on Long (1 seed). ACR-VLA uses $5{\times}$ fewer VLA forward passes than the $K{=}10$ methods. A boundary analysis on OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2024openvla} (7B, deterministic $L_1$ regression), where $97.3$\% of steps produce near-identical actions, confirms that stochastic diversity is a prerequisite.

\looseness=-1 The key finding is that \emph{gating}, not correction strength, is the mechanism. CRM always-on applies the same learned residual to every step, including the ${\sim}$80--90\% where the VLA is already confident---corrections on these steps are noise that averages out any benefit. ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers CRM only on high-uncertainty steps (trigger rate 4--20\%, varying with suite difficulty), preserving the VLA's own output elsewhere. This selective application turns a correction module that is harmful when unconditional into one that provides targeted improvement on uncertain suites while protecting confident ones.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{ACR-VLA pipeline} (Section~\ref{sec:method}): an adaptive $K{=}2$ uncertainty-gated correction pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. A lightweight CRM fires only when per-step uncertainty exceeds a calibrated threshold, using $5{\times}$ fewer VLA forward passes than $K{=}10$ methods.
  \item \textbf{Selective improvement} (Section~\ref{sec:main_results}): adaptive gating improves high-uncertainty suites ($+$1.0--2.1\,pp) while preserving baseline on confident ones, unlike unconditional correction ($-$1.3\,pp Object, $-$1.5\,pp Long).

4	\section{Applicability Boundary: Stochastic VLA Diversity}
5	\label{sec:applicability}
6	
7	\looseness=-1 The multi-sample pipeline requires stochastic action diversity across samples. We validate this prerequisite on two VLA architectures: SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} (flow matching, 0.4B) and OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2024openvla} (deterministic $L_1$ regression, 7B).
8	
9	SmolVLA produces meaningfully diverse action samples across all dimensions via its flow-matching generative process. In contrast, OpenVLA-OFT's deterministic $L_1$ regression produces near-identical outputs: mean pairwise $L_2{=}0.00436$ across $K{=}2$ samples, with $97.3$\% of steps below $0.01$. The uncertainty gate never fires, and multi-sample selection is vacuous.
10	
11	This result establishes an architectural boundary: multi-sample inference-time correction is specific to stochastic generative VLAs (flow matching, diffusion). Deterministic VLAs lack the action diversity that selection and correction rely on. The boundary is architectural, not a limitation of our method: any inference-time approach that draws multiple action candidates requires the base policy to produce diverse samples.
12

15	\label{sec:tau_sweep}
16

18	\centering
19	\caption{Threshold sensitivity on Goal suite (seed 42, $\varepsilon{=}0.2$). VLA-only baseline: 83.5\% (seed-matched). Optimal performance at $\tau{=}0.15$; the selected operating point $\tau{=}0.25$ trades peak single-seed improvement for a more conservative trigger rate.}
20	\label{tab:tau_sweep}

22	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
23	\toprule
24	$\tau$ & Trigger rate (\%) & SR (\%) & $\Delta$ vs VLA-only \\
25	\midrule
26	0.10 & 73.9 & 81.0 & $-2.5$ \\
27	0.15 & 33.9 & 85.0 & $+1.5$ \\
28	0.25 & 7--9 & 84.0 & $+0.5$ \\
29	0.40 & 1.2 & 83.5 & $0.0$ \\
30	\bottomrule
31	\end{tabular}

34	\looseness=-1 Table~\ref{tab:tau_sweep} reports success rates on Goal (seed 42) as a function of the uncertainty threshold $\tau$, with $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ (the adaptive correction magnitude). Performance follows an inverted-U pattern: at $\tau{=}0.10$ the gate triggers on 73.9\% of steps, overcorrecting confident ones and degrading performance by $-$2.5\,pp---reproducing the instability of unconditional correction. At $\tau{=}0.40$ the gate triggers on only 1.2\% of steps, effectively disabling the CRM and recovering VLA-only performance ($\Delta{=}0.0$).
35	
36	\looseness=-1 The optimal operating region is $\tau \in [0.15, 0.25]$, where 8--34\% of steps receive correction and success rate improves by $+$0.5 to $+$1.5\,pp over the seed-matched baseline. The main experiments use $\tau{=}0.25$, which sacrifices peak single-seed improvement for a more conservative trigger rate. The inverted-U shape confirms that gating selectivity---not correction strength---drives performance: too much correction is as harmful as too little.
37	
38	\looseness=-1 \textbf{Note on $\varepsilon$ comparisons.}\enspace The $\tau$-sweep uses $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ (the adaptive pipeline's norm bound). CRM always-on in Table~\ref{tab:main} uses a tighter $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ to limit overcorrection when applied unconditionally. The two settings are not directly comparable: CRM always-on ($\varepsilon{=}0.05$, 100\% trigger) achieves 85.5\% on Goal seed 42, exceeding $\tau{=}0.10$ ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$, 73.9\% trigger) at 81.0\%. This reflects the interaction between correction magnitude and trigger frequency---unconditional correction requires a gentler $\varepsilon$ to remain stable, while gated correction tolerates a larger $\varepsilon$ because it fires selectively.

On Object, where the VLA is already confident, the gate triggers on only 3.5\% of steps---the CRM barely fires, and the output matches baseline ($77.8$\%, $\Delta{=}0.0$, 3 seeds). This is the correct behavior: the gate identifies that Object needs no correction and avoids the $-$1.3\,pp harm of unconditional correction. On Spatial and Goal, where higher uncertainty triggers correction on 7--20\% of steps, the CRM provides targeted improvement ($+$2.1\,pp and $+$1.3\,pp respectively). Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can be improved at inference time without modifying weights, but existing approaches either apply correction unconditionally or invest in multi-sample selection without learned correction.
We propose ACR-VLA, a lightweight adaptive correction pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. At each control step, the pipeline draws $K{=}2$ action samples in a single batched forward pass and uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance ($\rho{=}0.9979$ vs.\ $K{=}10$ sample variance) as a per-step uncertainty gate. Low-uncertainty steps output the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; high-uncertainty steps apply bounded residual correction via a Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters). Batched $K{=}2$ matches single-sample latency (${\sim}$170\,ms), making the uncertainty signal computationally free.
On SmolVLA (0.4B) across four LIBERO suites, unconditional CRM correction is unstable ($+$1.1\,pp Spatial but $-$1.3\,pp Object, $-$1.5\,pp Long). ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers correction only on high-uncertainty steps (4--20\%), improving performance where the VLA is uncertain ($+$2.1\,pp Spatial, $+$1.3\,pp Goal, 3 seeds; $+$1.0\,pp Long, 1 seed) while remaining neutral on Object ($\Delta{=}0.0$, gating correctly abstains). ACR-VLA uses $5{\times}$ fewer VLA forward passes than $K{=}10$ methods. The key finding is that \emph{gating}---knowing when to correct---is the mechanism: selective correction outperforms both unconditional correction and selection-only approaches. A boundary analysis on a deterministic VLA (OpenVLA-OFT 7B) confirms that stochastic action diversity is a prerequisite.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\looseness=-1 Deploying a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model on a new task usually requires fine-tuning on task demonstrations, yet collecting that data is expensive and the resulting checkpoint may not transfer further. A more attractive route keeps the VLA frozen and improves action quality at inference time. Flow-matching VLAs~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} are well suited to this setting because each forward pass produces a stochastic action sample, enabling multi-sample selection and correction without retraining~\cite{snell2024scaling}. The naive approach draws $K{=}10$ samples and applies unconditional correction at every step, but most control steps are easy---and we show that correcting them adds noise without benefit.

\looseness=-1 Recent work touches parts of this question without answering it. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns a correction head on action chunks but applies it unconditionally and addresses temporal staleness rather than initial action quality. ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} quantifies uncertainty over frozen VLAs but does not learn a corrective residual. SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} uses reinforcement learning and therefore does not stay weight-frozen. VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} performs evolutionary search at $2.41$\,s per control step, ruling out closed-loop deployment. None address the core question: can a frozen VLA decide \emph{per step} whether it needs correction at all?

\looseness=-1 We propose \textbf{ACR-VLA}, an adaptive inference-time pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. ACR-VLA draws only $K{=}2$ samples in a single batched forward pass and uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance as a per-step uncertainty probe. This probe is well-calibrated: Spearman $\rho{=}0.9979$ against $K{=}10$ sample variance, whereas three alternatives all yield $\rho \leq 0.15$. When the probe falls below a threshold $\tau$, the pipeline outputs the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; when it exceeds $\tau$, a lightweight Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters, $<\!1\%$ of the backbone) applies a bounded residual.

\looseness=-1 On SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} (0.4B) across four LIBERO suites~\cite{liu2023libero}, unconditional CRM correction ($\varepsilon{=}0.05$) is unstable: $+$1.1\,pp on Spatial but $-$1.3\,pp on Object and $-$1.5\,pp on Long (1 seed). ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers correction only on high-uncertainty steps (4--20\%), providing improvement where the VLA is uncertain ($+$2.1\,pp Spatial, $+$1.3\,pp Goal, 3 seeds; $+$1.0\,pp Long, 1 seed) while remaining neutral where the VLA is confident (Object, 3.5\% trigger rate). $K{=}10$ argmin selection~\cite{chen2026reconvla} hurts on Goal ($-$2.9\,pp) and Long ($-$1.5\,pp); $K{=}2$ mean averaging offers no learned correction mechanism. ACR-VLA uses $5{\times}$ fewer VLA forward passes than the $K{=}10$ methods. A boundary analysis on OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2024openvla} (7B, deterministic $L_1$ regression), where $97.3$\% of steps produce near-identical actions, confirms that stochastic diversity is a prerequisite.

\looseness=-1 The key finding is that \emph{gating}, not correction strength, is the mechanism. CRM always-on applies the same learned residual to every step, including the ${\sim}$80--90\% where the VLA is already confident---corrections on these steps are noise that averages out any benefit. ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers CRM only on high-uncertainty steps (trigger rate 4--20\%, varying with suite difficulty), preserving the VLA's own output elsewhere. This selective application turns a correction module that is harmful when unconditional into one that provides targeted improvement on uncertain suites while protecting confident ones.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{ACR-VLA pipeline} (Section~\ref{sec:method}): an adaptive $K{=}2$ uncertainty-gated correction pipeline for frozen flow-matching VLAs. A lightweight CRM fires only when per-step uncertainty exceeds a calibrated threshold, using $5{\times}$ fewer VLA forward passes than $K{=}10$ methods.
  \item \textbf{Selective improvement} (Section~\ref{sec:main_results}): adaptive gating improves high-uncertainty suites ($+$1.0--2.1\,pp) while preserving baseline on confident ones, unlike unconditional correction ($-$1.3\,pp Object, $-$1.5\,pp Long).
  \item \textbf{Gating necessity analysis} (Section~\ref{sec:failure_modes}): correction without gating is unreliable across suites; selection without correction is insufficient. The adaptive gate is the essential component.
  \item \textbf{Applicability boundaries} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_vla}): stochastic VLA diversity is a prerequisite---deterministic VLAs produce near-identical samples ($97.3$\% of steps $L_2 < 0.01$) and lie outside scope.
\end{enumerate}
